source: Sequential Edge: Inverse-Entropy Voting Beats Parallel Self-Consistency at Matched Compute (arXiv 2511.02309)
finding: At matched token budget, k chains that each build on the previous attempt beat k independent chains with majority vote in 43 of 45 configurations (5 open models, 3 benchmarks).
numbers: 95.6% win rate. Each chain capped at 4096 tokens; 6 chains = 24,576 tokens on both sides. Largest gap: Qwen3-235B AIME-2025, 6 chains, 76.7% vs 30.0%. Many gaps are small (e.g. GPT-OSS-120B AIME-2024 about 61% vs 60%). Inverse-entropy weighted vote best in 29 of 30 sequential cases.
quote: sequential reasoning outperforms parallel approaches in 95.6% of configurations
limits: Open-source models only (GPT-OSS, Qwen3, Kimi-K2). AIME has 30 items so one item is 3.3 points. The 4096 cap may truncate independent reasoning chains and hurt the parallel arm. Preprint; no Claude or GPT-5 class model.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 1 only in part: for open reasoning models at equal tokens, iterating on a prior attempt beats voting over independent short chains. Voting is not the default best use of a token budget.

source: Wunderlich et al. (2026) Multi-Agent Reasoning Improves Compute Efficiency: Pareto-Optimal Test-Time Scaling (arXiv 2605.01566)
finding: Across 34 configurations and over 100 evaluations, self-consistency saturates early. At equal compute, debate and mixture-of-agents beat self-consistency.
numbers: MMLU-Pro: CoT 64.3% to MoA 71.4% (+7.1) at up to 20x CoT compute; self-consistency 68.7%, debate 70.0%. At equal budget debate +1.3 and MoA +2.7 points over self-consistency. Gains at 15-20x CoT budget by difficulty: easy +2.2, medium +8.5, hard +9.0. Llama 3.1 70B (8B for size check), temperature 0.7.
limits: Non-reasoning open Llama models; only MMLU-Pro and BBH. Answer chosen by highest log-likelihood in the pipeline. Gains cost up to 20x tokens.
agent_relevance: Voting gives most of the cheap gain; aggregation by further model calls costs much more and mostly helps on hard items. Spend repeat samples on hard items, not easy ones.

source: Ding (2026) When LLMs Agree, Are They Right? Auditing Self-Consistency and Cross-Model Agreement as Confidence Signals (arXiv 2607.08065)
finding: Agreement among a model's own samples is a weak, regime-dependent signal of correctness. It is worst for the most consistent frontier model, which is over-confident but no more accurate.
numbers: 53 runners, K=50 samples each, 265,000 samples, GPQA-Diamond and AIME, gpt-4.1 family at temperature 1.0. Spearman between agreement and majority-correctness 0.20 to 0.59. Small exploratory Claude check (haiku-4.5, sonnet-4.6, opus-4.7; 48 GPQA and 24 AIME items) showed the same recurring confident errors; shared wrong answers had mean agreement 0.85 (GPT) and 0.78 (Claude); p=.003 haiku, p=.005 sonnet, p=.07 opus (not significant); only 12 shared-wrong items.
quote: agreement is not accuracy: a model can agree with itself ... out of shared bias
limits: Single author, crowd-run design with varied prompts. Claude check is explicitly exploratory and small. Hard multiple-choice and integer tasks only.
agent_relevance: Gaps 9 and 10: a self-agreement threshold (such as 85%) is not a validated confidence cutoff for frontier models; high agreement can mean shared error. Use agreement to allocate more compute, not to certify answers.

source: Chen (2026) When Does Combining Language Models Help? A Co-Failure Ceiling on Routing, Voting, and Mixture-of-Agents Across 67 Frontier Models (arXiv 2606.27288)
finding: Any router, vote or cascade that outputs one member's answer cannot beat accuracy 1 minus delta, where delta is the rate at which every model is wrong on the same query. Average pairwise error correlation cannot identify delta.
numbers: 67 frontier models from 21 providers (including GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro). All-wrong tail underpriced by a calibrated single-factor model by about 2.5x on open-ended maths (90% CI 1.7 to 3.4, k=17); delta 0.052 vs predicted 0.023; 0.079 on execution-graded code. Free-response GPQA reopens the tail (delta 0.127). At matched quality a diverse low-delta ensemble beats a high-delta Self-MoA one.
quote: combining models rarely beats the single best model without a strong query-level routing signal
limits: Single author preprint. Compares different models, not repeated samples of one model. Abstract and introduction read; body tables not all checked.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 10: voting over samples of one model is capped by the shared all-wrong rate, and gain comes from models that fail on different queries. Supports diverse prompts or models over repeated sampling when answers are checkable.

source: Aitchison, Jeen, Shevlane, Day (2026) Diversity is the Strength of the AI Crowd (arXiv 2606.29661)
finding: On binary Metaculus AI Benchmark questions, frontier LLM forecasts are tightly correlated. At a fixed budget the best allocation never puts all samples on one model.
numbers: Five frontier forecasters plus a fine-tuned gpt-oss-120b; all allocations up to budget B=5 searched by brute force. Best B=5 mix: fine-tuned 2, Gemini 3 Pro 1, GPT-5 1, Grok 4 1, Kimi 0. Grok 4 ranked third alone but is the least replaceable member because of low correlation with the others.
limits: Q2 2025 tournament, small model pool, binary forecasting only. Diversity is across models, not across prompts or personas of one model. Exact Brier numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a second draw from the same model adds only a fraction of the information of a draw from a different model. Our agent has one model; the nearest lever is varying prompt and framing, which this paper did not test.

source: Turkmen, Buyukates, Bastopcu (2026) Don't Always Pick the Highest-Performing Model: An Information Theoretic View of LLM Ensemble Selection (arXiv 2602.08003)
finding: With correlated errors, picking the top-k most accurate models is not optimal. Ensemble accuracy saturates at an error floor set by correlation. A greedy mutual-information selection beats top-k at equal query budget.
numbers: Gaussian-copula model of correlated errors; tested on MedMCQA, MMLU and IMDB. The paper states it beats strong baselines on all three; per-dataset gains not extracted.
limits: Binary classification only. Only abstract and introduction read in detail.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: in theory, adding samples with the same errors has diminishing return; selection should reward new information, not only accuracy.

source: Kumar, Rathore, Moitra (2026) All Verdicts are Not Equal: Rethinking LLM Judge Reliability (arXiv 2610.12083)
finding: Six frontier judges, four benchmarks, five prompt formats, two orders, three temperatures, ten repetitions each. Verdicts change across identical replications and flip when order is swapped.
numbers: 7% to 17% of verdicts change across identical replications at temperature 0. Up to 98% flip when presentation order is swapped. One judge gave the same verdict on 100% of repeats yet matched ground truth only 51%. Judges: GPT-5.2, GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Gemini-2.0-Flash, Claude-Sonnet-4.6, Llama-3.3-70B. Accuracy ceiling 1 minus flip-rate/2 from position bias.
limits: Industry preprint. Pairwise preference benchmarks (JudgeBench, LLMBar and others), not agent-loop tasks. Per-judge cells are about 200 items and noisy.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 5: current Claude and GPT-5-class judges still show 7-17% self-disagreement and large order flips on hard pairs. A pairwise verdict in an agent loop must be run in both orders and treated as noise-prone.

source: Kumar et al. (2026) paradigm comparison inside All Verdicts are Not Equal (arXiv 2610.12083): direct pairwise vs FLASK decomposed rubric vs G-Eval holistic
finding: Paradigm choice shifted trustworthiness more than any single prompt-format change. Single-prompt multi-criterion (G-Eval) scoring improved the trustworthy-verdict rate more reliably than decomposed rubric voting (FLASK).
numbers: Direct vs FLASK vs G-Eval compared on JudgeBench and LLMBar for the six judges. Table values vary widely by judge and benchmark; I do not report a single pooled number.
quote: G-Eval-style single-prompt multi-criterion scoring improves T more reliably than decomposed rubric voting
limits: Closest LLM test of splitting a verdict into sub-judgments, but FLASK scores criteria and votes. It is not Kahneman's protocol (independent sub-judgments, holistic call made last and delayed). Not a direct test. Based on the paper's intro statement and table, not a full read of section 5.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open, with a warning: naive decomposition into criteria did not beat a holistic multi-criterion prompt for pairwise correctness. Test the mediating protocol on our own items before adopting.

source: Norman, Rivera, Hughes (2026) Reliability without Validity: Large-Scale Evaluation of LLM-as-a-Judge (arXiv 2606.19544)
finding: 21 judges from nine providers, 118 runs, about 541,000 judgments, up to the April 2026 frontier. Test-retest reliability above 0.95 coexists with large position bias in the same judge.
numbers: Exact-match agreement overstates chance-corrected kappa by 33 to 41 points on MT-Bench for every judge. Judge rankings shift by up to 14 places across benchmarks. Position bias above 0.10 in judges with retest above 0.95 (Qwen3 8B, Gemini 2.5 Flash). Verbosity bias below 0.011 for all 21 (versus 20-40% variance reported in 2023).
limits: Single research group. Pairwise and score judging on benchmarks; agent loops not tested.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 10: repeat-agreement is the wrong health check. Measure order bias separately. Verbosity bias has fallen on current judges, so older bias lists may overstate it.

source: Bellibatlu, Singh, Parashar, Joshi (2026) Instability Floors: Separating Bias from Noise in Fairness Audits of Clinical LLM Agents (arXiv 2609.03221)
finding: A clinical LLM agent changes its own action when nothing changes. This self-disagreement floor must be measured before reading any demographic difference.
numbers: 16 synthetic vignettes, 10 reruns, default sampling: action changed in 8.7% of replicate pairs; 2.2% for ICU escalation up to 17.9% for controlled-substance caution. Six models from five vendors: floors 2.5% to 23.7%, not ordered by size, vendor or hosting. Majority of 5 draws removed 39% of the floor (95% CI 18 to 64). Temperature 0: three of four local models showed no disagreement; a hosted model still did.
limits: Synthetic vignettes, not real patients; acceptable-action bands drafted by the authors. No human-clinician spread measured, so no direct human comparison.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: an LLM noise audit on a professional task exists but is small and has no human baseline. Also, a 5-vote majority removed only about 40% of the noise. Gap 9: 5 draws is not enough to remove most of the floor.

source: Xu, Hirasawa, Kozuno, Ushiku (2026) Am I More Pointwise or Pairwise? Position Bias in Rubric-Based LLM-as-a-Judge (arXiv 2602.02219)
finding: Scoring against a rubric acts like multiple choice and shows model-specific position bias; the order of criteria in a multi-criterion prompt is a second bias axis. Balanced permutation is statistically no better than random order averaging.
numbers: Six judges, four datasets. Changing rubric order alone flips the top-1 candidate on 15% to 41% of prompts. Some judges prefer the first option, others the last. Balanced permutation indistinguishable from random aggregation; improves human correlation only for strongly biased judges; a small number of random orderings suffices.
limits: Budget-matched ablations on the authors' datasets. Judge models not all frontier. Exact permutation counts not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a cheap coded fix exists: score with a few random orderings and aggregate. Criterion order inside a prompt is itself a noise source for any mediating-assessment protocol.

source: Brocai and Becker (2026) Pair Difficulty Matters: Rethinking Pairwise LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation and Consistency (arXiv 2609.37577)
finding: Position bias, transitivity violations and self-agreement are dominated by close-rank pairs, where errors cost little for ranking. Far-gap pairs decide ranking accuracy but barely move the usual proxies.
numbers: Argued under a Bradley-Terry model; validated by simulation and on two human-rated corpora. Proxies correlate only weakly with ranking accuracy against gold.
limits: Abstract and related work read; results section numbers not extracted. Concerns ranking recovery, not item-level accuracy.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 9: a flat self-agreement threshold is misleading because disagreement concentrates on near-tie items. Give near-ties more samples or a coded tie-break; do not tune the loop to raise overall self-agreement.

source: Shi et al. (2025) Judging the Judges: A Systematic Study of Position Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge (arXiv 2406.07791, v9 Nov 2025)
finding: Position bias is not random chance and varies with judge, candidate-quality gap and task. Three metrics: repetition stability, position consistency, preference fairness.
numbers: 15 LLM judges, MT-Bench and DevBench (22 tasks), about 40 solution-generating models, over 150,000 evaluation instances, pairwise and list-wise.
limits: Only abstract and introduction read; per-judge figures not extracted. Judge set may not include the newest models.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: supports treating the quality gap as the main driver of order flips (agrees with d12).

source: Yuan et al. (2025) Understanding and Mitigating Numerical Sources of Nondeterminism in LLM Inference (arXiv 2506.09501)
finding: Even under greedy decoding, changing batch size, GPU count or GPU type changes outputs. In reasoning models early rounding differences cascade into different chains of thought.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B in bfloat16, greedy: up to 9% variation in accuracy and 9,000 tokens difference in response length across GPU count, type and batch size. An FP32-compute pipeline (LayerCast) reduces it.
limits: Open 7B reasoning model on controlled hardware. Not a measurement of API-hosted frontier models.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: run-to-run variation in long reasoning chains is amplified by chain length. Temperature 0 does not give repeatability on shared hosted infrastructure.

source: Nicholson (2026) Quantifying nondeterministic drift in large language models (arXiv 2601.19934)
finding: Repeated identical prompts give different outputs at temperature 0.0 and 0.7. Metrics are lexical (unique output fraction, similarity, word count), not correctness.
numbers: gpt-4o-mini and llama3.1-8b, five prompt categories. The introduction quotes second-hand (citing Atil) that a 120B model gave identical outputs in only about 12.5% of runs.
limits: Small models, lexical metrics only, single practitioner. The 12.5% figure is from the literature review, not this paper's runs.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: output text varies on every call, so only answer-level or verdict-level agreement is meaningful for noise measurement. Weak evidence for frontier models.

source: Messina and Scotta (2026) Introducing Background Temperature to Characterise Hidden Randomness in LLMs (arXiv 2604.22411)
finding: Nominal temperature 0 still carries an implementation-dependent effective randomness, called background temperature, from batch-size variation, kernel non-invariance and floating-point non-associativity.
numbers: Defines T_bg and a protocol to estimate it; pilot on a pool of major providers. Pilot values not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 8: noise level depends on serving conditions, so a noise audit must be rerun per provider and date, not assumed from a paper.

source: Grove, Zald, Lebow, Snitz, Nelson (2000) Clinical versus mechanical prediction: a meta-analysis. Psychological Assessment 12(1) (abstract via Europe PMC, PMID 10752360)
finding: Mechanical (formula) prediction was on average about 10% more accurate than clinical prediction. Clinical was often as good as mechanical and rarely much better.
numbers: Mechanical substantially better in 33% to 47% of studies depending on analysis. Clinical substantially more accurate in only 6% to 16%. Superiority consistent across task, judge type and experience. Clinical did worse when interview data were included. The abstract does not state the study count.
quote: mechanical predictions of human behaviors are equal or superior to clinical prediction methods for a wide range of circumstances
limits: Only the abstract was opened, not the full paper. The earlier 46/48/6 split in claim K18 does not match the abstract and is dropped. Mechanical here means human health and behaviour prediction, not LLM judging. The 136-study figure is not in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partly closed. The effect is real and consistent but modest (about 10% on average), not a rout. Supports coded rules for the final combination of cues; no evidence on LLM judges versus coded rules.

source: Meta-analysis of lens-model studies: The Success of Linear Bootstrapping Models, 2016 (record via Europe PMC; authors not shown in the record)
finding: Replacing a human judge with a linear model of that judge's own policy was more successful than the judge, on average. Success was larger with objective criteria and not clearly tied to domain or expertise.
numbers: Meta-analysis of lens-model studies, bare-bones and artifact-corrected. Correction raised the estimated success of bootstrapping, so uncorrected estimates may be too low. No effect sizes in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Stand-in for Goldberg 1970, which I could not open; Goldberg's own numbers remain unverified.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partly closed: the bootstrapping effect (a model of the judge beats the judge) has later meta-analytic support, strongest for objective criteria. Consistency alone, without extra insight, helps.
